newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN to stand tough on contentious issues at WTO.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN to stand tough on contentious issues at WTO.

text.p: Southeast Asian ministers said on Saturday they were set for tough talks at the first World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting in Singapore next month over issues such as labour standards and investment guarantees.
"Our positions on these issues will be substantially maintained," Philippine Foreign Minister Domingo Siazon said.
But he predicted some compromise might be possible with developed Western powers without giving way on principles.

"What is important is to find a set of words...so that all parties involved can feel happy that there is a meeting point for all contending parties," he told reporters on the fringes of an informal summit of ASEAN leaders in Jakarta.
ASEAN groups Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam and Brunei, with Laos, Cambodia and Burma as obvservers.
Envoys to the WTO -- the world trade regulatory body -- dropped efforts on Friday to agree in Geneva on a declaration on global commerce up to the year 2000.
They left ministers to decide at the Singapore meeting opening on December 8 what to say on such issues as labour standards, investment guarantees, competition policy and textile markets.
One envoy in Geneva anticipated there would be "a real ding-dong (battle) between North and South in Singapore".
Singapore's Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar said the city-state as host nation would take a neutral position on the issues, but would play a role in bridging the differences.
"If (WTO) members can come with the correct spirit, we will be able to do so," he told Reuters.

The declaration to be issued by the WTO's 125 member countries is supposed to underline the commitments of their governments to open up their national markets for goods and services into the 21st century.

Key developing countries in Asia oppose the inclusion of any reference to a link between labour standards and trade, or to suggestions that discussion on rules for investment and competition policy should enter the WTO agenda.

The United States and Norway, the most vocal proponents of bringing the labour conditions debate into the WTO, put their own texts for the declaration on the issue in Geneva but ran up against total opposition from India, Pakistan and ASEAN members.
"There are a lot of conflicting interests as far as the WTO goes," Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi said on Saturday in Jakarta.
"There will be some tough negotiations to go through," he said, but added that he did not consider the failure to reach an agreement in Geneva as a setback.
"Obviously, the officials (in Geneva) were not able to come to a conclusion that was acceptable to all," he said. "What officials cannot agree on will be passed on to ministers."

A Brunei trade official who is part of the tiny oil-rich kingdom's delegation to the ASEAN summit echoed the grouping's stand on labour issues being raised at the WTO gathering, but added that a compromise solution might not be reached.
"I don't know...if there will be a trade-off. It is too difficult to say at this moment because the gap (over differences) is too wide," he told Reuters.
Labour issues are not trade-related and that is the ASEAN perspective, he said.
